definition: In an indirect or roundabout way, without saying something plainly.
example: The coach mentioned the missed practices only obliquely, asking whether everyone's calendar was working.
nuance: Obliquely suggests a deliberate sidelong approach to a topic, while evasively implies dodging a question to avoid blame or commitment.
prompt: A guest at a dinner party wants to leave early without seeming rude.
options: She referred obliquely to an early meeting, hoping the host would take the hint.
She declared obliquely, "I am leaving now because this party is dull."
She was obliquely exhausted, yawning loudly every few minutes at the table.
She obliquely agreed to wash every dish before the dessert was served.
reasons: Hinting at a reason instead of announcing a departure is a sidelong, indirect approach.
A blunt, explicit announcement is the opposite of an indirect one.
This confuses the word with "obviously"; loud yawning is plain to see, not roundabout.
This confuses the word with "obligingly"; helpful agreement has nothing to do with indirectness.

practice.prompt: A novelist wants readers to sense a widow's grief without the narrator naming it.
options: The widow obliquely sobs on every page, so no reader could possibly miss her pain.
The author obliquely finished the whole manuscript in three weeks to meet a deadline.
The author conveys the sorrow obliquely, through the second teacup the widow still sets out each morning.
The author obliquely writes in chapter one, "Maria is overwhelmed with grief."
reasons: Open weeping on every page makes the grief unmistakable, which reverses the meaning.
How fast a book was written says nothing about approaching a subject indirectly.
A telling detail lets readers infer the feeling without it ever being stated.
Naming the emotion outright in a flat statement is a direct method, not an indirect one.
